source: Poddar, Sahoo, Ghosh (2025) Understanding Syllogistic Reasoning in LLMs from Formal and Natural Language Perspectives
finding: Belief bias is still present in 2025 models, but very uneven. Strong frontier models show almost none. Mid-size and small models show a lot. Switching on thinking mode did not remove it in the one matched pair.
numbers: 14 models, 160 syllogisms, 4 prompt strategies x 3 temperatures (N=6720 instance evaluations per strategy test). Congruent minus incongruent accuracy, points: Llama 3.2 3B +46.9; Llama 3.3 70B +31.6; Qwen3-Next 80B Thinking +28.0 (86.3 vs 58.3); Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite +12.5; DeepSeek V3.1 +7.9; Kimi-K2 +7.5; GLM-4.6 +1.9; Gemini 2.5 Pro +1.4 (100.0 vs 98.6); Gemini 2.5 Flash +0.9; GPT-OSS-20B +0.8; Qwen3-Next 80B Instruct -7.9 (75.5 vs 83.4); Gemma 3 27B -13.7. 12 of 14 models positive. Mean +10.81, SD 16.32, t13=2.47, p=.028, d=0.66. Few-shot mean 79.1 below zero-shot 82.7 (paired t41=2.50, p=.0165).
quote: Contrary to conventional wisdom, we find that few-shot prompting degrades performance compared to zero-shot
limits: Only 40 base syllogisms (160 with variants). The thinking vs instruct pair is one pair of different checkpoints, not a budget sweep. Models called through cheapest-route providers. Adaptive majority voting, so not single-shot behaviour. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 2, partly: the belief effect on top models is small to zero on syllogisms. A thinking label alone does not guarantee it (Qwen3-Next Thinking +28). A belief-debias step is not worth tokens on a strong model; it is for weaker or mid models. Few-shot examples can hurt.

source: Abe, Ozeki, Ando, Morishita, Mineshima, Okada (2026) Evaluation of Deontic Conditional Reasoning in LLMs: Wason's Selection Task (design re-read for gap 3)
finding: The deontic vs descriptive comparison is not a paired rewrite of one logical form. Deontic items are everyday norm rules ('if blood is spilled, the nurse must wear gloves'). Descriptive items are arbitrary card rules ('odd number, then uppercase letter'). So modality wording, topic familiarity and card format change together. Gap 3 cannot be answered from this paper.
numbers: 160 problems = 80 deontic + 80 descriptive; 20 per polarity pattern (pos-pos, pos-neg, neg-pos, neg-neg). Deontic gain over descriptive, +5 to +45 points by model and prompt (Table 2, e.g. qwen3-14b zero-shot 97.5 (+45), gpt-oss-20b zero-shot 67.5 (+27.5), gemma3-4b zero-shot 17.5 (+5)). Selection rates for gpt-oss-20b zero-shot on deontic rules, TA/FA/TC/FC: pos-pos 100/0/45/55; pos-neg 100/0/5/95; neg-pos 80/20/60/40; neg-neg 90/10/10/90. Authors conclude errors fit matching bias better than confirmation bias. Exact-match multi-select; temperature 0 for non-reasoning models.
quote: Overall, these findings suggest that LLMs exhibit domain-specificity effects in reasoning with deontic rules
limits: Content, modal word and format are confounded, so the +5 to +45 gain cannot be split into content vs 'must' wording. Matching-bias analysis shown in the main text for one model.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open. Cheap test to run: 2x2 of (norm content vs arbitrary content) x (must/plain-is wording) on the same four-card logic. Until then, treat the LLM deontic advantage as content plus wording, not proven content.

source: Cosmides (1989) The logic of social exchange: Has natural selection shaped how humans reason? Studies with the Wason selection task. Cognition 31, 187-276 (Experiments 1-2)
finding: Original numbers for the famous result. Unfamiliar social contracts (standard form) got about 3 in 4 correct P and not-Q. Unfamiliar descriptive rules and the abstract rule got about 1 in 4. This argues against simple familiarity (availability) as the cause.
numbers: Exp 1 and Exp 2: 24 Harvard undergraduates each, paid volunteers. P and not-Q, Exp 1 / Exp 2: unfamiliar standard social contract 75% / 71%; unfamiliar descriptive 21% / 25%; abstract 25% / 29%; familiar descriptive 46% / 38%. Contrasts: 75 vs 21, F(1,23)=27.18, r=.74; 71 vs 25, F(1,23)=19.46, r=.68; social contract vs abstract 75 vs 25 (r=.61) and 71 vs 29 (r=.65). Drinking-age problem: 78% in a similar Harvard group (n=23).
limits: Within-subject, a few problems per person, one lab defending the theory. n=24 gives wide error bars.
agent_relevance: Closes the original-numbers question for Cosmides 1989. The effect is large only when the rule has a clear cost-benefit and the goal is to catch a violator. Stating the violation condition is the transferable part.

source: Cosmides (1989) Cognition 31 (Experiments 3-6 and 8-9: switched contracts and non-social-contract permission rules)
finding: Switched social contracts flip the card choice (not-P and Q), which formal logic and a general permission schema do not predict. Permission rules without a cost-benefit structure did much worse than social contracts. This is the main evidence against Cheng and Holyoak's permission schema. The often-quoted '65 to 80 percent' comes from these experiments.
numbers: Exp 3, 4 (n=24 each): correct switched social contract answer not-P and Q 67% and 75%. Exp 5, 6 (n=40 each, Stanford): standard social contract P and not-Q 75% and 80% vs non-social-contract permission rule 30% and 45% (z=2.85, phi .45; z=2.29, phi .36). Exp 8, 9 (n=40 each): switched social contract not-P and Q 65% and 80% vs 0% and 10% for the switched non-social-contract permission rule on that response. Author summary: 75 to 80% vs 30 to 45% (standard); 65 to 80% (switched).
limits: OCR text with errors in some lines; only clean numbers are used. Author is the theory's originator. Harvard and Stanford students only.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 closed for Cosmides 1989; gap 8 origin found: '65 to 80' is the range over Cosmides' own Exps 1 to 9 (n=24 or 40 each). It is not by itself evidence of stability across labs.

source: Cosmides (1989) Cognition 31: her report of Cheng and Holyoak (1985) Experiment 2 (second-hand for the 61 vs 19 figure)
finding: The 61 vs 19 figure is now traced to a source that was read in full, but it is still second hand. In Cheng and Holyoak's second experiment, using only the first problem each person saw, the abstract permission rule got 61% P and not-Q vs 19% for the letter-number rule. Their first experiment was clouded by transfer between problems.
numbers: 61% vs 19% (abstract permission vs concrete letter-number rule, first problem only). Same passage: drinking-age problems usually get about 75% P and not-Q.
limits: Cheng and Holyoak 1985 itself was not opened (the Michigan link returned an HTML page, not the PDF). N per cell is still unknown. Cosmides is a rival theorist.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 half closed: report 61 vs 19 as a figure reported by Cosmides, N unknown. Holyoak and Cheng 1995 add that Exp 1 showed the identical rule gave facilitation only when context made it an established regulation to check for violations.

source: Kroger, Cheng, Holyoak (1993) Evoking the permission schema: the impact of explicit negation and a violation-checking context. Q J Exp Psychol 46A, 615-635
finding: A rival explanation (Jackson and Griggs 1990) said the abstract-permission gain came only from two presentation tricks: explicit 'not A' cards and a violation-checking frame. Here the same tricks were given to an arbitrary rule and did nothing, while the permission rule gained a lot. So both the frame and the deontic meaning matter.
numbers: Exp 1A (UCLA and Univ. of Washington students), correct P and not-Q: violation-checking with explicit negatives: permission 47% (n=38) vs arbitrary 5% (n=40), chi2(1)=18.35, p<.001. Violation-checking without explicit negatives: permission 18% (n=45) vs arbitrary 8% (n=40), n.s. Hypothesis-testing frame with negatives: 16% (n=36) vs 6% (n=36). Exp 2 (131 UCLA students), no explicit negatives: permission 22% vs arbitrary 6%, chi2(1)=8.37, p<.005. Partial replication, 124 students: 32% (n=71) vs 8% (n=53). Telling readers the arbitrary rule was a conditional, not a biconditional, did not help.
quote: No facilitation was observed for an arbitrary rule even when explicit negatives and a violation-checking context were used
limits: Authors are the permission-schema group. Gains are fragile: large only with the full recipe (violation frame plus explicit negatives).
agent_relevance: Gap 9, human side. Ingredients that matter together: say the goal is to find violations, write the not-P and not-Q cases explicitly, and use a rule that reads as a regulation. A 'restate as what counts as a violation' step supplies the first two.

source: Gigerenzer and Hug (1992) Domain-specific reasoning: Social contracts, cheating, and perspective change. Cognition 43, 127-171 (Part 1: replication and cueing)
finding: An independent lab (Konstanz) replicated Cosmides' unfamiliar social-contract effect and found it larger. The same social-contract rules gave only about 44 to 45% when the question did not cue the party who can be cheated. So the effect depends on the question asked, not only the rule type.
numbers: n=93 Konstanz students, two rules (cassava, duiker). P and not-Q: cheating version 94% vs no-cheating 44% (50-point gap; Cosmides Exp 1: 75% vs 21%). Permission rules, cheating vs no-cheating cue: 89% vs 53% (overnight), 77% vs 46% (Grover), mean +33 points. Obligation rules: 89% vs 41%, 77% vs 38%, mean +44 points. Social-contract rules without a cheater cue averaged 45%, about the same as non-social-contract rules (44%).
quote: The crucial issue is not semantic (the meaning of the rule), but pragmatic
limits: German students, written materials. Authors support the theory but separate it from a 'cheater algorithm'. They do not explain why Konstanz students exceeded Harvard students by about 20 points.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 partly closed: an independent lab, same direction, similar or larger size (gap of 33 to 50 points). For the agent: the question it asks ('who could be cheated, and what would show it') changes the answer. Build a fixed slot for whose violation is being checked.

source: Gigerenzer and Hug (1992) Cognition 43 (Part 2: perspective change with bilateral cheating options)
finding: For one and the same rule, swapping the reader's point of view swaps the cards chosen, from P and not-Q to not-P and Q. Same logic, same words, opposite answers.
numbers: Day-off rule: employee view P and not-Q 75%, employer view not-P and Q 61%; the reverse choices were 2% and 15%. Pension rule (n=93): P and not-Q 70% vs 11% for the two perspectives; not-P and Q 0% vs 64%. Subsidy rule: P and not-Q 81% vs 17%, not-P and Q 59% vs 0%.
limits: Single lab, students. A later critique (seen only in a search summary, not opened) says the effect reduces to domain knowledge within logical reasoning.
agent_relevance: A schema step 'state whose violation is being checked' is a direct, cheap test. Matches K04.

source: Sperber, Cara, Girotto (1995) Relevance theory explains the selection task. Cognition 57, 31-95 (Experiments 1-3)
finding: Primary numbers for the relevance claims. Changing only the story, so the rule reads as something to deny rather than confirm, lifts correct P and not-Q from a low base to a majority on descriptive rules.
numbers: Exp 1 (virgin mothers, 27 Paris VI students, within-subject): P and not-Q 78% vs 26% in the standard task, McNemar chi2(1)=12.07, p<.001. Exp 2 (bachelors, Trieste): relevance n=17 65% vs irrelevance n=19 16%, z=2.96, p<.01. Exp 3 (unemployment, Paris X, n=20 per cell): 70% vs 25%.
limits: Small cells (17 to 27). Authors are the theory's authors. The standard-task baseline in Exp 1 (26%) was above the usual 10%, which they suspect is transfer.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partly closed from the primary paper (Ragni et al. 2018 Table 4 still unopened). Relevance manipulations give 40 to 50 point gains on descriptive rules, as large as deontic content gains. The mechanism is whether the reader expects a counterexample to exist. A restatement 'what would show this rule false' may carry it.

source: Sperber, Cara, Girotto (1995) Cognition 57 (Experiment 4: machine problem, effect x effort)
finding: Two separable factors drive good selection on an abstract task: how much the conditional suggests a denial (effect) and how easy the not-Q case is to represent (effort). One factor gives about 38%, both favourable gives 57%, neither gives 5%.
numbers: Exp 4, 84 first-year psychology students at Padua, n=21 per condition. P and not-Q: effect+/effort- 12 of 21 (57%); effect+/effort+ 8 of 21 (38%); effect-/effort- 8 of 21 (38%); effect-/effort+ 1 of 21 (5%). Main effect of effect z=2.5 and of effort z=2.5, both p<.01, no interaction; 57% vs 5%: z'=3.6, p<.001.
limits: Small n, one lab. The effort manipulation is subtle card wording.
agent_relevance: Gives a recipe for a form-extraction prompt: ask for the case that would falsify the rule and name the not-Q case explicitly. Matches K06 and K10.

source: Ahn and Graham (1999) The impact of necessity and sufficiency in the Wason four-card selection task. Psychological Science 10(3), 237-242
finding: Best human evidence found for 'state the logical relation of the rule before reasoning'. When the rule was written with its necessity and sufficiency explicit, ordinary students gave the card pattern that fits that relation, including on abstract letter-number rules.
numbers: Exp 1: 22 Yale undergraduates, 4 materials x 4 versions, Latin square. P and not-Q 50% when unnecessary-but-sufficient vs 0% when necessary-but-insufficient; not-P and Q 59% for necessary-but-insufficient; all four cards 55% for necessary-and-sufficient. Control (relation unspecified): P and not-Q 18%, not-P and Q 14%, all four 18%, P alone 23%. On the abstract letter-number rule 50.0% of responses over the three explicated conditions were normative, equal to social material (57.1%). Exp 2: 23 Yale students pitted the necessity-sufficiency account against the cheater-perspective account; result not extracted.
quote: When necessity-sufficiency relations were explicated, normative responses were elicited
limits: Within-subject. Added 'might' or 'must' and context stories, so wording and relation change together. Small N. The normative answer is relative to the stated relation, not the classic material conditional.
agent_relevance: Good candidate wording for the restatement operator: 'what does the rule say is needed, and what is enough'. Gap 1 and 9 get human support only; no LLM test.

source: Macchi, Poli, Caravona, Vezzoli, Franchella, Bagassi (2019) How to get rid of the belief bias: boosting analytical thinking via pragmatics. Europe's J Psychol 15(3), 595-613
finding: A one-phrase change in the task question ('Does the conclusion necessarily follow from the premises?') hugely cut belief bias on an invalid-but-believable syllogism, in logic-trained and untrained students. Logic training alone did nothing without the phrase.
numbers: Exp 1 control ('Does the conclusion follow?'), 130 students (50 untrained, 80 logic-trained): correct on the invalid-believable syllogism 4% untrained, 10% trained. Exp 2 'Necessarily' instruction: 66% untrained, 77% trained. 'Criteria of Logic' instruction: 41% untrained, 67% trained (chi2(2,N=80)=4.91, p=.03). Control vs Necessarily: chi2=42.24 (untrained) and 47.91 (trained), p<.001.
limits: Two syllogisms per person; one invalid-believable item. A 'Why?' question followed in all conditions. Earlier instruction attempts often failed or did not replicate (their Table 1: 92/8%, 75/83%, 81/56%).
agent_relevance: Restating what 'valid' means can beat belief. Test: add 'necessarily follows; ignore whether it is true in the world' to the agent's own question. Costs no extra tokens.

source: Nguyen, Tachibana, Liu, Liu, Noe, Takeda, Kurohashi (2026) BIS Reasoning 1.0: Japanese benchmark for belief-inconsistent syllogistic reasoning (v5, Table 1, Sec 4.2)
finding: Reasoning models are near ceiling on valid but belief-inconsistent syllogisms. The same small model drops by 30 points when its reasoning effort is set to minimum. So reasoning effort, not size, is the lever in this test.
numbers: Accuracy on BIS / NeuBAROCO belief-inconsistent: GPT-5-mini medium effort 99.72 / 91.92; GPT-5-nano medium 98.84 / 91.32; GPT-5-nano minimum effort 69.22 / 73.05; gpt-oss-20b 98.56 / 89.52; GPT-4o 79.54 / 94.01; GPT-4-turbo 59.48 / 67.66; Qwen3-32B no thinking 99.58 / 94.01, thinking 99.12 / 97.60; Claude-3-sonnet 20.34 / 78.44; Claude-3-opus 7.18 / 61.07 (deprecated models).
limits: Japanese data. Only one item type (valid, belief-inconsistent), so a general lean to say 'invalid' is not separated from skill; no matched belief-consistent control in the table. One zero-shot prompt.
agent_relevance: Gap 2, partly: a budget lever exists (GPT-5-nano 69 to 99 between minimum and medium effort), but Qwen3-32B reaches 99 without thinking. The lever matters mostly for weaker or chat-tuned models. Supports S3 budget being conditional on model.

source: Nguyen et al. (2026) BIS Reasoning 1.0, Sec 4.3: GPT-4o error re-test with different prompts (Fig 4-5, Table 2)
finding: Closest LLM test of a restatement-type prompt. Among 100 syllogisms GPT-4o had got wrong, a prompt telling it to focus strictly on the logical relation and whether the conclusion follows necessarily recovered 76%. Step-by-step CoT recovered 87%. The plain prompt recovered 5%.
numbers: 100 GPT-4o error cases re-run: basic 5%, casual 3%, polite 65%, focus-logic 76%, chain-of-thought 87%. English prompts on the same Japanese data gave a similar order with smaller gaps.
quote: Explicit logical instructions or chain-of-thought prompting significantly reduce belief bias
limits: Only failed items were re-tested (selection effect; rerun noise looks low because basic stays at 5%). No equal-token comparison: CoT uses more tokens than the focus-logic prompt. No 'restate the violation' arm and no thinking-budget model. One dataset and language.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM evidence for gap 1: a short instruction naming the task as strict logical necessity recovers most of what CoT does (76 vs 87%) at far fewer tokens. Not a fair test yet; both were not run at equal tokens on all items.

source: Ranaldi, Valentino, Freitas (2025) Improving Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via Quasi-Symbolic Abstractions (QuaSAR), ACL 2025
finding: A prompt that has the model name the relevant variables and predicates, rewrite the problem in a mix of symbols and words, then explain and answer, gave small to moderate gains over plain CoT on large models and changed less under surface perturbations. It hurt small models.
numbers: GPT-4o, CoT vs QuaSAR accuracy: AQuA 84.3 vs 87.4; GSM8K 94.5 vs 96.5; SVAMP 90.3 vs 97.0; MMLU-Redux 88.1 vs 90.2; OlympiadBench 41.8 vs 44.6; GPQA 50.2 vs 55.4; DROP 84.2 vs 88.9. Text: improvement 19.1% for GPT-4o, 11.8% for Llama-3-70B, 17.2% for Qwen2-72B over baseline. Dropping the formalise or explain step cost more than 3.5 points on average. On GSM-Symbolic and shuffled-option MMLU-Redux QuaSAR varied less than CoT (Table 4, text description only). Small models (Llama-3-1B, 8B, Qwen2-1.5B, 7B) did worse than CoT as in-context learning.
limits: The table text was garbled; GPT-4o rows came from raw extraction, with the order baseline, CoT, other methods, QuaSAR assumed. Token cost not reported. Temperature 0. The target is robustness to surface change, not human-like content effects.
agent_relevance: Gap 6, partly: prompt-only abstraction works on GPT-4o-class models with less variance under changes, but token cost is unmeasured, and small models lose. Not shown to beat an equal-length CoT.

source: Gao, Bosselut, Bengio, Abbe (2026) AbstRaL: Augmenting LLMs' Reasoning by Reinforcing Abstract Thinking. ICLR 2026
finding: Abstracting a word problem to symbols and mapping back reduces name and number sensitivity on GSM tasks, but the model needed RL training to abstract faithfully; supervised training often gave unfaithful abstractions. Other abstraction-style baselines scored far below plain CoT on a strong 7B model.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct, GSM-Symbolic Vary Both: AbstRaL 90.2 (drop from original 100 problems 0.86%) vs CoT-8S 87.7 (7.73%) vs CoT-RL 88.1 (8.21%); CoA 69.7 and AoT 70.4. Qwen2.5-0.5B: AbstRaL 44.6 (drop -1.27%) vs CoT-8S 34.0 (10.6%). GSM-Plus distractor set, 7B: AbstRaL 82.3 vs CoT-8S 76.3.
limits: Needs RL fine-tuning, SymPy and a larger LLM for condition recognition (replacing tools with the model itself costs little in their ablation). Small open models up to 8B, math word problems only.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: a pure prompt version of 'abstract, solve, map back' is not shown to work here; QuaSAR (d15) is the prompt-only evidence. Keep the abstraction operator optional, with a map-back check.

source: Valina, Seoane, Ferraces, Martin (1996) Wason's selection task: content effect, instruction effect or both? (Third International Conference on Thinking)
finding: Violation-checking instructions do not always help. They helped the thematic permission rule but not the obligation or abstract versions; instruction x content interaction on the logical index was significant. The review also reports Platt and Griggs: an abstract rule with violation instructions, an explained rule and a request for reasons reached about 80% correct.
numbers: Per-cell N and percentages not extracted from the text read. Platt and Griggs (1995) 'around 80%' is second hand.
limits: Conference paper. Platt and Griggs 1993 and 1995 not opened.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a violation-framing step is not a universal fix; its effect depends on how deontic the rule already looks. Make it conditional on rule type and test per type.

source: Stanovich and West (1998) Cognitive ability and variation in selection task performance. Thinking and Reasoning 4(3), 193-230 (abstract seen in a search result only)
finding: Per the abstract: in three studies with over 800 participants, non-deontic selection tasks were solved disproportionately by people of higher cognitive ability, while two deontic tasks (drinking-age, Sears) were unrelated to ability. Deontic and nondeontic scores were consistently associated.
numbers: More than 800 participants over three studies. No effect sizes obtained.
limits: Not opened as a paper; the file link returned an HTML stub. A later review says ability predicted deontic tasks worse but effects were mostly in the right direction and sometimes significant.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays mostly open. If it maps to models, strong reasoners gain more on abstract tasks and show smaller content effects. That fits d01 and d13 (top models near zero belief effect), but no source tests it on the Wason task.

source: Ayman, Marzouk, Mashaly, Hereiz (2026) Proofbusters at SemEval-2026 Task 11: Neuro-Symbolic Syllogistic Reasoning via LLM-Guided Structure Extraction and Deterministic Validation
finding: A two-stage 'extract the form, then judge the form' pipeline cut the content effect to near zero on English syllogisms. Template masking (All x are y) helped less than a set-notation translation. The comparison baselines were weak small models, not a strong model asked directly.
numbers: Official English subtask. Set-theoretic (Gemini 2.5 Flash formulates, Gemini 2.5 Pro solves): accuracy 98.95, total content effect (TCE) 2.13, official score 46.23. Accuracy of the other arms: Gemma3-7B zero-shot 71.70; Gemma3-270M fine-tuned 74.00; template abstraction 82.20; object-oriented abstraction 88.84. Dropping the existential-import constraint: 98.95 to 80.00. Solver token cap 512. T=0.
quote: deeper mathematical abstraction fully stripping semantic content and leveraging formal set notation substantially outperforms template-based approaches
limits: No direct-prompt or plain-CoT arm with the same Gemini models, so the gain over a strong model asked directly is not measured (see d21: a strong model alone scores 98.43). No token cost. Task labels follow Aristotelian existential import, which the scoring depends on. Score column of the table was garbled in extraction; accuracy values are reliable.
agent_relevance: Extract-the-form works as a pipeline, but this paper cannot say it beats a strong model reasoning directly. Treat as evidence for weak or mid models only.

source: Akinfaderin, Diallo (2026) FregeLogic at SemEval 2026 Task 11: A Hybrid Neuro-Symbolic Architecture for Content-Robust Syllogistic Validity Prediction
finding: A solver used only as a tiebreaker on split ensemble votes gave a small gain. A solver used alone or with veto power was much worse, because the LLM step that extracts the logical form fails on valid items. Prompt type mattered: minimal CoT had the lowest content effect, and few-shot CoT raised it for one model.
numbers: N=960 items, nested 5-fold CV, 192 test items per fold. Ensemble of 5 LLM classifiers (Llama 4 Maverick, Llama 4 Scout, Qwen3-32B): accuracy 93.4 +/- 1.5, CE 3.39 +/- 1.30. Plus Z3 tiebreaker on 3-2 splits: 94.3 +/- 0.9, CE 2.85 +/- 1.23, score 41.88 vs 39.12. Z3 only: 74.7, CE 26.28. Z3 veto: 74.1, CE 26.70. Z3 alone: 97.6 on invalid but 52.2 on valid items. 3-2 splits: 76 of 960 (7.9 percent); Z3 overrode 30, 19 correct and 11 wrong, net +8 items. Extraction failures fell from about 22 percent to near zero with structured output. Cost: 5 ensemble calls plus 1 extraction, about 4,300 tokens and 12.1 s per syllogism. Simple CoT had the lowest average CE (5.24); for Maverick few-shot CoT raised CE from 3.83 to 10.11 vs few-shot.
quote: Z3-only baseline exhibits a pronounced invalidity bias
limits: Gain of 0.9 accuracy points and 0.54 CE is inside one standard deviation across folds. Net +8 items out of 960. Models are 17B to 32B active parameters, not frontier. Cost is not compared to a single strong model with more thinking.
agent_relevance: Hybrid benefit on belief-inconsistent items is real but tiny and costs about 6 calls. The extraction step is the weak link, the same step an 'extract the form' operator would rely on. Never let a solver veto; use it only where checks disagree.

source: Muhamad, Lopo, Wong, Habibi, Cahyawijaya (2026) ITLC at SemEval-2026 Task 11: Normalization and Deterministic Parsing for Formal Reasoning in LLMs
finding: With a strong model (Gemini 3 Flash preview), asking directly already gave 98.43 percent and a content effect of 2.13 on English syllogisms. Rewriting to canonical syllogism form and parsing with fixed rules reached 100 percent and zero content effect. The gain over a direct strong model is under two points.
numbers: English validity (n=192 test): LLM-only 98.43, CE 2.13, score 45.74; normalise + deterministic parsing 100, CE 0.0. Multilingual validity: LLM-only 96.87, CE 4.16; normalise + parse 96.88, CE 3.12; with English pivot translation 100, CE 0.0. Normalisation formats on English (Table 1, split not stated): raw 92.10 / CE 10.63; predicate-argument 77.48; first-order logic 96.85 / 3.19; syllogism notation 98.95 / 2.13 (these two numbers equal Proofbusters' official row, so check before quoting). Relevance-premise subtask: LLM-only 95.78 vs parsing 98.94.
limits: One model. Syllogisms only; moves the content effect from about 2 to about 0. No token counts. The normalisation step is itself an LLM call, so 'deterministic' covers only the second stage.
agent_relevance: Headroom is small once the model is strong. A form-extraction step is most useful for weaker models or for the last point of content effect, not as a default.

source: Kartac, Onderkova, Bronec, Kasner, Lango, Dusek (2026) UFAL-CUNI at SemEval-2026 Task 11: An Efficient Modular Neuro-symbolic Method for Syllogistic Reasoning
finding: For a 4B reasoning model (Qwen3 4B Thinking), translating to first-order logic and handing the proof to a prover beat asking the model to judge validity itself, by about 12 points. Letting the same model do the proof step on the logic formulas gave back most of the loss. The 4B model translated well but reasoned badly.
numbers: Subtask 1 (English), Qwen3 4B Thinking: full pipeline accuracy 95.83, CE 2.28, score 45.61. Zero-shot end-to-end 84.17 (CE and score garbled in extraction). LLM as prover on the formulas: 79.22, CE 20.21, score 19.58. Parsing straight to Prover9 syntax instead of via LaTeX: 85.97, CE 12.23, score 24.11. Single-step vs multi-step formalisation: 95.81 vs 95.83. Qwen3 4B beat the 30B-A3B variant; Instruct and Thinking 4B were comparable. About 18 percent of direct-syntax formulas had syntax errors.
limits: Small models, one task, benchmark labels have errors (10 of 21 validation errors were wrong labels). Token cost not reported. Table rows partly garbled; accuracy and the three CE values that reconcile with the score formula are reliable.
agent_relevance: For small models, move the logical step out of the language model. The worth of a solver rises as the model gets weaker or the proof gets longer; the break-even is not yet known for a strong model.

source: Valentino et al. (2026) SemEval-2026 Task 11: Disentangling Content and Formal Reasoning in Large Language Models (overview), Table 2 and Sec. 4
finding: In the shared-task baselines, belief bias does not shrink steadily with model size. Qwen3 8B and 14B were near ceiling with small content effects, while older 7B to 14B models had content effects of 30 to 45 points. About 250 teams took part, with over 3,000 submissions and 35 system papers.
numbers: Subtask 1, no special interventions (accuracy / total content effect): Qwen3 14B 97.38 / 4.23; Qwen3 8B 95.81 / 4.23; Phi-4 15B 83.33 / 14.89; Qwen2.5 14B 67.50 / 44.54; Gemma3 7B 71.70 / 29.75; Llama 3.1 8B 64.17 / 32.15; Llama 3.2 3B 57.64 / 29.81. A second 'Qwen3 8B' row (78.00 / 21.10) is a different participant run. English test set: 192 items, balanced over valid/invalid x plausible/implausible.
limits: Numbers are participant-reported under different prompts. Scores mix prompts, so they are not a clean size scaling. Test set is small and built by LLM generation with manual checks.
agent_relevance: Supports 'model generation and reasoning training predict the content effect better than size'. Gate any debias step on the measured gap of the model in use.

source: Nguyen et al. (2026) BIS Reasoning 1.0, Table 1 and Sec. 4 (re-read for single-model contrasts)
finding: The only within-model effort contrasts found: GPT-5-nano lost 30 points when reasoning effort went from medium to minimum, while Qwen3-32B was at ceiling with or without thinking. All items are belief-inconsistent, so there is no congruent control and no true gap.
numbers: BIS Reasoning 1.0 / NeuBAROCO belief-inconsistent accuracy: GPT-5-nano medium 98.84 / 91.32; GPT-5-nano minimum 69.22 / 73.05; GPT-5-mini medium 99.72 / 91.92; gpt-oss-20b 98.56 / 89.52; Qwen3-32B without thinking 99.58 / 94.01; Qwen3-32B with thinking 99.12 / 97.60; GPT-4o 79.54 / 94.01; GPT-4-turbo 59.48 / 67.66. Same 'Basic' yes/no prompt for all.
quote: substantial differences in performance arise depending on how inference-time reasoning capacity is activated and utilized
limits: Two effort levels only. No token counts. Basic prompt asks for a bare yes or no, so low-effort models cannot reason in text (the authors say GPT-4o's internal deliberation may have been suppressed). Japanese data, translated NeuBAROCO subset of over 300 items.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open: no sweep over many budgets on one mid-size model, and no congruent items. Budget helps where there is room, which is mid-size models with a bare-answer prompt.

source: Maraia, Valentino, Zanzotto, Ranaldi (2026) Abstract Activation Spaces for Content-Invariant Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Zero-shot CoT improved bias-penalised accuracy a lot on 7B to 14B models but left a large residual, and for Mistral-7B it barely helped. Steering toward activations of the abstract version of each syllogism (All A are B) did far better. Steering needs model weights, so it is not a text scaffold.
numbers: English test (2,780 paired items, 3-fold CV). Bias-penalised accuracy (accuracy x (1 - belief gap)), baseline / steered / zero-shot CoT: Qwen-2.5-7B 50.8 / 95.4 / 81.7; Qwen-3-14B 72.3 / 97.8 / 83.1; Gemma-2-9B 51.8 / 98.0 / 69.9; Gemma-3-12B 79.4 / 97.0 / 86.8; Mistral-7B 30.2 / 96.1 / 34.3; Ministral-14B 63.9 / 97.6 / 76.2. Averages: 58.1 / 97.0 / 72.0. Steering gains +16.5 to +43.0 BPA; Mistral-7B +65.9.
limits: CoT and fine-tune baselines were run on fold 0 of some models only (the paper says so); steering is averaged over 3 folds. No token counts. Cannot be done with API-only models. Metric mixes accuracy and gap.
agent_relevance: Shows a text-only CoT leaves a gap that the model's own internal 'abstract' representation can close. Supports the idea that form extraction has headroom, but gives no evidence that a prompt can reach it.

source: Abe, Ozeki, Ando, Morishita, Mineshima, Okada (2026) Evaluation of Deontic Conditional Reasoning in LLMs: The Case of Wason's Selection Task (EACL short; design re-read for gap 3)
finding: Confirmed from the full text: deontic rules are those with obligation or prohibition words (must, need to, must not, not allowed); descriptive rules are arbitrary if-then generalisations with no modal word. So rule type, content and modal wording all differ between conditions. Permission and 'need not' rules were left out because the correct cards differ.
numbers: 160 problems: 80 deontic, 80 descriptive, 20 per polarity pattern (p-q, p-not q, not p-q, not p-not q). Items were generated by Gemini 1.5 Pro from templates and then hand-checked. Deontic-minus-descriptive accuracy (zero-shot): gpt-oss-20b +27.5, gpt-oss-120b +30, qwen3-14b +45, qwen3-32b +38.8, gemma3-4b +5, llama-3.3-70b +10. Deontic accuracy zero-shot: gpt-oss-120b 100.0, qwen3-32b 98.8, qwen3-14b 97.5, gemma3-4b 17.5. Non-reasoning models: output cap 10 tokens for zero and few-shot, 6,000 for CoT; reasoning models 6,000 to 11,000. Exact-match multi-select. Few-shot exemplar answers were deliberately wrong for the test items.
limits: One exemplar pair per type in few-shot. No test of the same logic with and without 'must', and no norm-free deontic. Authors list permission/obligation work as future work. Temperature 0 for non-reasoning models only.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 is not closed. The deontic gain could come from norm content, from 'must', from the story format, or from all three. Design for the 2x2 in K22 holds.

source: Seals, Shalin (2024) Evaluating the Deductive Competence of Large Language Models (NAACL 2024)
finding: Older 7B models showed a smaller social-rule advantage than humans, and it interacted with presentation format in non-human ways. The design used matched stimulus sets with arbitrary, realistic and shuffled-content rules, social and non-social. It is the closest published thing to a content-by-rule-type control for LLMs, but it does not vary the modal word.
numbers: 70 social-rule and 70 non-social-rule problems (35 familiar and 35 unfamiliar in each). Models: Guanaco, MPT, BLOOM, Falcon (about 7B), plus larger Llama2, Wizard, Falcon and Guanaco sizes in an appendix. Scored by DCPMI (chance 1/6). Realistic vs shuffled content: odds ratio 1.30 [1.05, 1.62]. Social-rule status x content interaction: OR 1.59 [1.26, 2.02]. Realistic non-social vs realistic social: OR 0.33. Switched social rules scored well below standard ones, as in Cosmides 1989. LLMs solved social-rule problems about 30 percent of the time, vs about 70 percent for humans.
limits: Old, small models and log-likelihood scoring, not chat or reasoning models. Item N is small. Familiarity and model identity did not improve model fit, so results are pooled.
agent_relevance: Gives a template for the paired design but no answer about 'must'. A switched-contract check is a cheap, theory-backed test that an agent's pass is not just matching the word 'must'.

source: Fiddick, Cosmides, Tooby (2000) No interpretation without representation: the role of domain-specific representations and inferences in the Wason selection task. Cognition 77, 1-79 (Experiment 1)
finding: People still chose P and not-Q on a trade problem when no if-then rule and no modal word were stated at all (villager says 'I want potatoes', farmer says 'I want corn'). The content effect therefore does not need the logical connective or a 'must'. This is a human result from the group that defends the social-contract view.
numbers: N=60 UCSB students and staff, 30 per group. P and not-Q: Conditional version ('If you give me potatoes, then I will give you corn') 66.7 percent; Want version (no rule stated) 50.0 percent. P only: 20.0 vs 13.3. Question was 'see whether any of the villagers have cheated the farmer'.
limits: Advocate lab. Small N. An unfamiliar trade scenario, one item. The final question ('cheated') carries the violation framing, so it is not content alone.
agent_relevance: For humans, violation-aware framing in the question did the work without any modal word. The 2x2 in K22 should keep the final question fixed, or add a fifth cell that changes only the question.

source: Fiddick, Cosmides, Tooby (2000) Cognition 77 (Experiment 2: standard vs precaution question, same descriptive rule)
finding: The same descriptive rule gave 16.7 percent P and not-Q under a truth-seeking question and 50.0 percent when the goal was to find people endangering themselves. Changing only the goal sentence moved the answer by about 33 points, with the rule text identical and no obligation stated.
numbers: N=60, 30 per group. Rule: 'If you go hunting, then you wear these jackets to avoid being shot' (a statement of function, not a norm). P and not-Q: Standard 16.7; Precaution 50.0. Standard also gave P only 26.7, P and Q 23.3. Precaution gave P only 20.0.
limits: Advocate lab, one scenario, 30 per cell, no inferential test copied here. Authors read it as evidence for a hazard-management module; relevance theory could read it as a goal change.
agent_relevance: Strong human support for putting an explicit 'what counts as a violation' goal into the task restatement (O1). Not tested in LLMs; this is exactly the equal-token test in gap 1.

source: Holyoak, Cheng (1995) Pragmatic reasoning with a point of view. Thinking and Reasoning 1(4), 289-313
finding: The permission-schema authors say the modal word matters in their own theory: 'must' rules mark a violation as definite, while 'may' rules mark no violation as possible, which blocks the wrong card choices. They also say a cost-benefit setting is only one case of the rationale that makes a rule a regulation, and they dispute the reading of Platt and Griggs (1993), who found that removing the cost-benefit context from social-contract rules cut facilitation.
numbers: No new data here. Cites Cheng and Holyoak (1985) as showing facilitation for an abstract permission rule ('If one is to take action A, then one must first satisfy precondition P') and Cheng and Holyoak (1989) for an abstract precaution rule. Gigerenzer and Hug (1992) violation-check vs hypothesis-test context replicated Yachanin and Tweney (1982) and Cheng and Holyoak (1989).
limits: Theory review by the authors of the theory under test. The 1985 numbers are still second hand; the Michigan repository PDF was blocked by a bot check and was not opened.
agent_relevance: In schema theory, 'must' is part of the mechanism, so a content effect and a 'must' effect are not separable even in principle; a clean test needs the 'may' versus 'must' cell too.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in Large Language Models, Tables 1 to 3 and Sec. 4 (full text)
finding: The gain of Step-Back over zero-shot CoT is much smaller than the gain over the plain prompt, and for GPT-4 on MMLU it is within about one standard deviation. On StrategyQA Step-Back was slightly below CoT. Step-Back also adds a second call that produces the abstract question.
numbers: MMLU Physics / Chemistry, accuracy (sd over runs). PaLM-2L: CoT 65% (2%) / 75.3% (1.5%); Step-Back 73.2% (1.9%) / 81.8% (1.4%); so +8.2 and +6.5 over CoT. GPT-4: plain 69.4% (2.0) / 80.9% (0.7); CoT 82.9% (0.5) / 85.3% (1.0); Step-Back 84.5% (1.2) / 85.6% (1.4); so +1.6 and +0.3 over CoT. PaLM-2L TimeQA: CoT 40.8, Step-Back 66.0. MuSiQue: CoT 38.7 (3.2), Step-Back 42.6 (3.1). StrategyQA: CoT 83.6 (0.4), Step-Back 82.7 (0.4). The authors report that Step-Back fixes errors but introduces a small portion of new ones (at most about 12 percent) and that the reasoning step stays the main bottleneck.
limits: Models are PaLM-2L, GPT-4 (2023) and Llama2-70B. No token counts, no equal-compute arm. Tasks are STEM and fact lookup, not content-effect tasks.
agent_relevance: On a strong model, abstraction over plain CoT is a small gain on STEM. It was not tested on belief bias. Gap 4 is partly answered: the gain over CoT is small and token cost is unreported.

source: Chen, Chi, Wang, Zhou (2024) Premise Order Matters in Reasoning with Large Language Models (ICML 2024)
finding: Models do best when the premises appear in the order of the proof (forward order). Random order cuts accuracy sharply. The paper shows the effect and a best case, but does not test a prompt step that re-orders premises before answering.
numbers: Deductive tasks on GPT-4-turbo, GPT-3.5-turbo, PaLM 2-L, Gemini 1.0 Pro. Shuffling can lose over 30 percent; for Gemini 1.0 Pro and GPT-3.5-turbo from over 65 percent to below 25 percent in some settings (a drop over 40 points). GPT-4-turbo and PaLM 2-L drop up to 20 to 30 points. R-GSM (GSM8K with reordered statements), original vs reordered accuracy: GPT-4-turbo 94.1 to 85.0; PaLM 2-L 86.4 to 79.5; Gemini 1.0 Pro 80.5 to 69.1.
limits: 2023 to 2024 models; no reasoning models; the best order uses the ground-truth proof, which is not known at test time. No reorder-step arm.
agent_relevance: K28 sensitivity is confirmed from the full text, but 'a reorder step helps' is still untested. The reorder would need the model to find the proof order, which is the hard part.

source: Trippas, Thompson, Handley (2017) When fast logic meets slow belief: Evidence for a parallel-processing model of belief bias. Memory and Cognition 45, 539-552
finding: In humans the belief effect depends on task complexity. For the simplest problems (modus ponens), belief judgments were less accurate than logic judgments. For the most complex three-term multiple-model syllogisms, belief interfered more with validity judgments than the reverse. A logic-only judgment still carried a conflict cost.
numbers: Experiment 1 (45 students recruited; two removed before analysis; modus ponens and tollens). Accuracy by judgment type, conflict vs no conflict: MP belief .63 vs .93, MP logic .73 vs .97; MT belief .67 vs .91, MT logic .69 vs .86. Overall conflict .68 vs no conflict .92 (chi2(1)=39.7, OR 2.88). Experiment 2 (84 students) used problems of rising complexity.
limits: Student samples, one lab. The argument is about parallel versus default-interventionist models; any link to LLMs is only by analogy.
agent_relevance: Human boundary condition: telling people to judge only logic does not remove the conflict cost, and belief gains ground as problem complexity rises. A scaffold should add checking with problem complexity and not assume an instruction suffices.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Human-derived instructions to consider counterexamples raised the success rate of LLMs on an interactive rule-discovery task, from 42 to 56 percent on average over 11 models. Thinking mode gave more success but did not consistently lower confirmation bias, and thinking models used about 1,000 or more tokens per turn against about 6 to 24 for non-thinking models.
numbers: Eleven LLMs; task success 6 to 78 percent within 45 turns. Qwen3-32B thinking: about 1,030 tokens per turn at baseline and about 1,450 with the Think-in-Opposites instruction. Dual-Goal improved success in 8 of 11 model-setting cases. 80 episodes per point. Distilling the intervention behaviour into the model generalised to a new task (Blicket test).
limits: Different task (interactive rule discovery, not Wason cards). The results table was partly garbled in extraction, so per-cell success rates were not copied. The instruction raises token use, so the accuracy gain is not at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: A rare case where a human debiasing instruction was tested in LLMs with token use shown: it helps but costs more tokens. Equal-token controls are needed before crediting the instruction.

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta, Chan, Sheahan, Creswell, Kumaran, McClelland, Hill (2024) Language models, like humans, show content effects on reasoning tasks. PNAS Nexus 3(7)
finding: On the natural language inference task, a few examples took Chinchilla from content-biased to near ceiling, and even a simple instruction substantially reduced the bias; on the Wason task both humans and models were forced to pick exactly two cards, and the realistic-rule advantage showed in every model. Removing the pre-question instructions did not change the main results.
numbers: Models: Chinchilla, PaLM 2-M and 2-L, Flan-PaLM 2, GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct. Wason: slow human responders above chance on realistic but not arbitrary rules; two of the larger models above chance on arbitrary rules. Scoring by log-likelihood of answer choices with a DC-PMI correction.
limits: Forced two-card choice and log-likelihood scoring differ from free-text multi-select in Abe et al. (d26). Old models. The authors note that a sequential-reasoning route (CoT) may behave differently from the likelihood route.
agent_relevance: Instruction sensitivity is part of the original finding; the scaffold's value must be measured against a strong plain instruction, not against a bare prompt.
